Changing a password stores it as plain text, so `argon2.verify` can never match it at login.

**How it happens**
1. `PUT /user` calls `userService.update(userId, userData)` with the raw request body (`src/user/user.controller.ts:26-29`). No validation pipe is applied to this route. `main.ts` registers no global pipe either, and only `create` and `login` use `@UsePipes`.
2. `update()` runs `delete toUpdate.password`, which only removes the old hash from the loaded object. It then does `Object.assign(toUpdate, dto)` and `save()` (`src/user/user.service.ts:74-81`). `UpdateUserDto` has no `password` field (`src/user/dto/update-user.dto.ts`), but a TypeScript type strips nothing at runtime. A `password` in the body is copied onto the entity and saved as typed.
3. Hashing happens only in `hashPassword()`, which is marked `@BeforeInsert()` (`src/user/user.entity.ts:28-31`). There is no `@BeforeUpdate`, so the update path never hashes.
4. At login, `findOne()` calls `argon2.verify(user.password, password)` (`src/user/user.service.ts:31`). That compares the typed password against a plain-text value that isn't an argon2 hash, so it fails. The controller then returns 401 (`src/user/user.controller.ts:48`).

This matches LESSONS.md #88 and the "Password change path" item in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md:13`, which is still unchecked.

**Affected users and recovery**
- Everyone who has changed their password through `PUT /user` has plain text in the `password` column.
- Those rows are readable as-is, so it is also a security problem, not just a login bug.
- I can't tell how many users are affected from the code. You'd have to look at the database for `password` values that don't start with `$argon2`.
- Recovery means a forced reset or re-hash for those users, because the plain-text value is whatever they typed. A one-off migration that hashes any non-`$argon2` value would work.

**Fix I'd propose**
- In `update()`, hash explicitly with `argon2.hash` when a password is supplied.
- Copy only the allowed fields by name instead of `Object.assign` (LESSONS #112). This also closes the problem where `id` or any other field in the body gets persisted.

I haven't changed any code. Do you want me to make that fix? The data cleanup for already-affected users is a separate decision, because it touches production data.

I didn't read `auth.middleware.ts`, so I haven't ruled out an auth-side contribution. The read-only symptom (login fails only after a password change) fits the hashing path above.
